evals.prompt: Define React composition patterns as a discipline in 2-3 sentences. Name the core patterns and what problem they solve.
expected_elements: Frames it as growing a component API by composition instead of accumulating boolean flags
Names the core patterns: compound components, explicit variants, children-over-render-props, and the provider state/actions/meta interface
States the problem solved: boolean prop proliferation / state-space explosion / fragile conditional rendering
Mentions composition keeps valid states explicit and enumerable as the component scales

evals.prompt: Why is each boolean prop described as a multiplier on a component's state space, and what does that imply about adding 'just one more boolean'?
expected_elements: Each boolean doubles the combined state space (n booleans -> 2^n combinations)
Most of those combinations are impossible, unsupported, or contradictory
Adding a boolean is a cost (untested combinations, brittle conditionals), not a free feature
The real shape of the component is the set of named valid variants, not the cartesian product of flags

evals.prompt: When should an agent reach for a compound component (shared-context children) versus an explicit variant component? What does each buy and cost?
expected_elements: Compound components fit a family of parts that share state (e.g. Tabs.List/Tab/Panel) coordinated through a provider
Explicit variants fit a fixed set of named modes that would otherwise be flag combinations
Compound components trade some API ceremony for flexible, prop-drill-free composition
Explicit variants trade a larger named surface for eliminating impossible flag combinations

evals.prompt: A Button component has props isPrimary, isLoading, isDisabled, isGhost, and isIcon. Walk through how the skill says to refactor it.
expected_elements: Run the boolean state-explosion audit: 5 booleans -> 32 combined states, most impossible
Inventory flags, enumerate valid combinations, delete impossible states
Name the remaining valid states as explicit variant components
Add an example or test per valid variant

evals.prompt: Describe the provider state/actions/meta interface and why decoupling implementation from consumers matters.
expected_elements: The provider is the single place that owns and knows how state is managed
It exposes a generic interface of state, actions, and meta
State is lifted into the provider so siblings access it without prop drilling
Consumers depend on the contract, not the implementation, enabling dependency injection / swapping internals

evals.prompt: A teammate asks this skill to stop a component tree from re-rendering too often by adding memoization. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Not in scope — render-performance optimization (memoization, suspense, profiling) belongs to a React performance skill (react-best-practices)
This skill owns the component's API shape, not its render speed
Correctly distinguishes API composition from rendering optimization
Offers to redirect performance work to the owning skill

evals.prompt: An engineer says 'more props makes the component more flexible, so I'll just add another boolean.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: More booleans mostly add fragility, not flexibility — each one doubles the state space and most combinations are invalid
Real flexibility comes from composition: explicit variants, a provider, and children composition
At 3+ booleans, treat the API as broken until the state-explosion audit proves otherwise
Adding a boolean is a cost (untested combinations, brittle conditionals), not a free win

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a component has been correctly refactored using these composition patterns?
expected_elements: No component has 3+ boolean props without an explicit variant refactor
State is lifted into a context provider, not drilled through props
Compound components use children composition, not renderX props
Impossible state combinations are documented and eliminated; each valid variant has an example or test
React 19 code passes ref as a regular prop and uses use() instead of useContext()
